## Where people and schools are {#sec-distance-places}

All locations are on the British National Grid, in metres, so distance is simple geometry and needs no map projection.

**Neighbourhoods.** The unit is the 2021 Lower Layer Super Output Area (LSOA), of which England has `r format(Pm$n_lsoa, big.mark = ",")`. An LSOA is placed at the mean of the population-weighted centroids of its Output Areas (`r format(Pm$n_oa, big.mark = ",")` in England). That puts it where people live rather than at the middle of its land, which matters for large rural LSOAs. Averaging the Output Area centroids gives each Output Area equal weight, rather than weighting by its population. The two are close, since Output Areas are built to be of similar size, and the measure from Output Areas directly is one of the checks.

**Schools.** A school counts as secondary if its type group in GIAS is an academy, free school or local authority maintained school, its phase is secondary, all-through or middle deemed secondary, and it takes pupils at 13 or younger and keeps them to at least 16. This leaves out special schools, pupil referral units, independent schools, 16 to 19 colleges and university technical colleges that start at 14. Primary schools, used only for the falsification test, are those of primary, all-through or middle deemed primary phase.

GIAS is used rather than the KS4 performance tables because the tables have no coordinates for 165 schools, mostly all-through, and miss schools too new to have a GCSE cohort. That omission affected an earlier version of this analysis.

**The network each year.** Each year's network is the schools open that September: opened by 30 September and either still open or closed after 1 September. An academy conversion closes the old school number on 31 August and opens a new one on 1 September, so a converting school is counted once. All `r Pm$no_grid` closed secondary schools with no grid reference closed by 1994, so none affects these years. Schools that moved site carry their current location throughout, because GIAS does not keep earlier ones.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-distance-network
#| tbl-cap: "State-funded secondary schools in the network each September, and authorities with absence by disadvantage that year. Authorities are fewer in earlier years because DfE's data then use boundaries since reorganised, which are not matched to 2023 authorities."
Rm$network_n |> left_join(Rm$n_la_year, by = "tp") |> transmute(`School year` = year, Schools = format(schools, big.mark = ","), Authorities = ifelse(is.na(authorities), "–", as.character(authorities))) |> kt(align = "lrr")
```

## Measuring distance {#sec-distance-measures}

**Nearest school.** For each neighbourhood $i$, the distance $d_i$ to the nearest school $s$ in the set $S$ is

$$d_i = \min_{s \in S} \sqrt{(x_i - x_s)^2 + (y_i - y_s)^2}$$

found with a k-d tree nearest-neighbour search (`nabor::knn`). It is a straight line and takes no account of roads, hills, the sea or admission rules.

**The most deprived third.** Within each place, neighbourhoods are ranked by the share of households deprived in two or more of the Census's four dimensions (employment, education, health, housing), and the top third by number of neighbourhoods form the set $T$. The place's measure is the mean of $d_i$ weighted by $w_i$, the number of 10 to 14 year olds:

$$D_{T} = \frac{\sum_{i \in T} w_i d_i}{\sum_{i \in T} w_i}$$

and the same for the other two-thirds, $D_{R}$. The ratio $D_T / D_R$ is the "how much further" on the page. The third is taken within each place, so it means "most deprived for here", not an absolute level. Places are 2023 districts and upper-tier authorities with at least 30 LSOAs, which drops the Isles of Scilly and City of London.

**Kind of place.** The ONS 2021 Rural Urban Classification of each neighbourhood. A place is "mostly urban" if at least 80% of its 10 to 14 year olds live in urban neighbourhoods. `r sum(Dm$authorities$urban_share >= 80)` of `r nrow(Dm$authorities)` authorities are. Others are "less urban".

**The eleven versions.** `R/19_distance_absence.R` recalculates the measure for each authority and year in these ways:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-distance-versions
#| tbl-cap: "The measures of distance from an authority's deprived neighbourhoods."
tibble::tribble(
  ~Measure, ~Calculation,
  "Nearest school (headline)", "The mean distance for the most deprived third, D<sub>T</sub>, as above",
  "Nearest school, logged", "log<sub>2</sub> of D<sub>T</sub>, so the slope is for each doubling",
  "Mean of the three nearest", "Distance from each neighbourhood is the mean distance to the three nearest schools, since many children do not go to their nearest",
  "Nearest neither selective nor faith", "The set of schools leaves out schools with selective admissions or a religious character, which many children cannot or would not attend",
  "Nearest, from Output Areas", "Distance is measured from each Output Area and weighted by its children up to the LSOA",
  "Deprived in one or more dimensions", "The third ranks neighbourhoods on one or more dimensions rather than two or more",
  "Most deprived fifth", "The set is the top fifth rather than the top third",
  "England's most deprived third", "The set is the neighbourhoods in England's most deprived third, wherever they are, if an authority has at least five",
  "Weighted by household deprivation", "All neighbourhoods, weighted by 10 to 14 year olds times the share of households deprived",
  "Weighted by child poverty (IDACI)", "All neighbourhoods, weighted by 10 to 14 year olds times the IDACI score: the distance for a typical child in income deprivation",
  "Share of children over 2 km", "The share of children in the most deprived third living over 2 km from a school, in points"
) |> kt(align = "ll", escape = FALSE)
```

These measures are in different units, so [the specification curve](distance.qmd#sec-curve) expresses slopes per standard deviation of the measure across authorities in that year.

**A school's nearest children.** How far each school's pupils travel is not published. As a stand-in, each Output Area is assigned to its nearest school, which divides the country into Voronoi cells. A school's measure is the mean distance of its assigned Output Areas, weighted by their 10 to 14 year olds, and it is recalculated each year. Schools nearest for fewer than 100 children and selective schools are left out. Many pupils go elsewhere, so this describes where a school sits among children rather than who attends.

**IDACI on 2021 neighbourhoods.** DfE's residence file uses the 2019 IDACI, which is published on 2011 LSOAs. The ONS lookup links them to 2021 LSOAs: in England `r format(Pm$lsoa_change$U, big.mark = ",")` links are unchanged, `r format(Pm$lsoa_change$S, big.mark = ",")` are splits, `r Pm$lsoa_change$M` merges and `r Pm$lsoa_change$X` more complex changes. Each 2021 LSOA takes the mean score of its linked 2011 LSOAs, and its national tenth comes from the score boundaries of the published tenths. No LSOA is left without a score. Children by tenth and authority, built this way, correlate at `r sprintf("%.3f", Pm$corr_cells)` with DfE's pupils by tenth and authority, which is the check that the two line up. Our IDACI is still an approximation for neighbourhoods whose boundaries changed.

## Absence {#sec-distance-absence}

- **Rates.** Overall absence is sessions missed as a percentage of sessions possible, calculated from DfE's counts. Illness uses authorised illness sessions, and unauthorised uses unauthorised sessions, over the same denominator. Persistent absence is the percentage of enrolments missing 10% or more of sessions.
- **Disadvantaged pupils** are those DfE records as eligible for free school meals in the last six years, and non-disadvantaged pupils those not. The share disadvantaged is calculated from their enrolments, separately by phase and year.
- **Two geographies.** The characteristics file places pupils where they go to school and the residence file where they live. So the within-authority tests are the closer match to home neighbourhoods. Children crossing authority boundaries add noise to the first.
- **School files** cover the autumn and spring terms, which is why their rates differ from full-year figures. Schools are followed through changes of number using the links in GIAS, as on [How school absence changes](absence_change.qmd).

## The models {#sec-distance-models}

**Authorities.** For authority $a$, year $t$ and each group of pupils:

$$A_{at} = \beta D_{at} + \gamma' X_{at} + \tau_t + \varepsilon_{at}$$

where $A$ is absence, $D$ the distance measure, $X$ the controls and $\tau_t$ a year effect. Single-year models use robust (HC3) errors. Pooled models cluster errors by authority. One check allows errors to be correlated between authorities within 100 km (Conley). The authority-effects model adds $\alpha_a$ and so uses only changes in the network over time.

**Controls.** They are built up in sets, used in [the specification curve](distance.qmd#sec-curve):

1. Share of pupils disadvantaged, and percentage of 10 to 14 year olds in urban neighbourhoods.
2. Region (the nine English regions).
3. Census character of the authority: graduates (level 4 and above), bad or very bad health, White British residents, social renting, households with no car or van, households deprived in two or more dimensions, and the child-weighted mean of log population density.
4. Pupils in the authority's secondary schools, weighted by size, from January 2026: SEN support, EHC plans, prior attainment, English as an additional language, White British share and mobility. These are one year's values applied to every year.
5. The same group's primary absence in the same year.

Some of these could lie on the path from distance to absence rather than confound it, such as density and car ownership, so the fullest models may take away part of what they are trying to measure.

**The specification curve.** Every combination of year, measure, control set and sample (all authorities, without London, mostly urban, mostly urban without London, less urban), for each group of pupils and phase: `r format(nrow(Rm$curve), big.mark = ",")` models. The share "above zero" describes sensitivity to these choices, not statistical evidence. The models share data and are far from independent.

**Ethnic mix of each group.** From DfE's counts of pupils by ethnicity and free school meal eligibility, for each authority, phase and year: the shares of a group who are White British, Asian, Black and of mixed heritage, out of those with a recorded ethnic group. Pupils known to be eligible stand in for disadvantaged pupils and those not for non-disadvantaged pupils, since DfE counts current eligibility here and eligibility in the last six years in the absence file. DfE's published categories are used, with Asian including Chinese.

**What takes the slope away (Gelbach decomposition).** Let $b_0$ be the slope on distance given share, urbanity and year, and $b_1$ the slope when controls $z_k$ are added. Then

$$b_0 - b_1 = \sum_k \hat\gamma_k \hat\delta_k$$

where $\hat\gamma_k$ is the coefficient on $z_k$ in the full model and $\hat\delta_k$ the slope of $z_k$ on distance in the base model. This is an identity, so the parts add up exactly and do not depend on the order of the controls (Gelbach, 2016, *Journal of Labor Economics*). Parts are summed into blocks, with intervals from 300 bootstrap samples of authorities. It describes how the slope changes, and does not by itself show which controls are confounders and which mediators: that needs the reasoning on the Distance page.

**Within ethnic groups.** The authority model, on absence for each ethnic group, for authorities with at least 100 pupils in that group, with distance from the deprived neighbourhoods and from where the group lives: $\sum_i n_{ei} d_i / \sum_i n_{ei}$ over all the authority's neighbourhoods, where $n_{ei}$ is the group's Census residents of all ages. DfE does not split these figures by disadvantage.

**Direct standardisation.** For all pupils, expected absence for an authority is $\sum_e p_{ae} r_e$, where $p_{ae}$ is the share of its pupils in each of DfE's minor ethnic groups and $r_e$ is that group's national rate in that year. The slope of actual absence on distance then splits exactly into the slope of expected absence (mix) and the slope of actual minus expected (beyond mix).

**The primary test.** The same model on primary absence, and on secondary minus primary absence for the same authority, year and group. The difference absorbs anything about a place that affects both phases equally.

**Within authorities.** For pupils in authority $a$ and IDACI tenth $k$:

$$A_{akt} = \beta D_{akt} + \gamma' C_{akt} + \alpha_{at} + \kappa_{kt} + \varepsilon_{akt}$$

where $D_{akt}$ is the child-weighted distance from the authority's neighbourhoods in that tenth, $C$ is their Census character, and $\alpha_{at}$ and $\kappa_{kt}$ are effects for each authority and for each tenth, by year. So $\beta$ asks whether, in an authority, the tenths that are further from a school than the national pattern for those tenths have higher absence than expected. Groups with fewer than 30 pupils are dropped, models are weighted by pupils and errors are clustered by authority. Between-authority versions leave out $\alpha_{at}$.

**Schools.** For school $s$ in year $t$, with $\log_2$ of the nearest-children distance $N$:

$$A_{st} = \beta \log_2 N_{st} + \delta (\log_2 N_{st} \times F_{st}) + \gamma' Z_{st} + \lambda_{at} + \varepsilon_{st}$$

where $F$ is the free school meals share, centred, and $Z$ is SEN support, EHC plans, English as an additional language, girls, log size and kind of place. A further version adds the school's White British share from the January 2026 census, held fixed across years because these files do not give earlier shares. Year-by-year models use authority effects. School-effects models replace them with an effect for each school, so $\beta$ uses only schools whose nearest children's distance changed. In those models $\delta$ is mostly driven by free school meals changing at schools whose distance did not, and among the `r Rm$sch_fe_moved$schools` schools with a change of 10% or more its estimate is not clear, so it is not reported as a response to network change.

## What these calculations cannot do {#sec-distance-limits}

- **The people are grouped, not individual.** DfE publishes no absence by disadvantage below authority level, and no disadvantage split in the residence file. The disadvantaged pupils in an authority do not all live in its most deprived third, so $D_T$ is a proxy for their distance, and these tests can differ from what would be found for individual children.
- **Ethnic groups are broad.** Each combines very different communities, and they stand in for much that is not measured. Nothing here says why attendance differs between them. Pupil ethnicity is not split by disadvantage in the absence data.
- **Census and IDACI are fixed.** Deprivation, children and Census character are from 2021, and IDACI from 2019, in every year. Only the school network and absence change.
- **Straight lines are not journeys,** and the nearest school is not always attended.
- **Network changes are not experiments.** Schools open where populations grow, and few authorities' distances changed much.

## Journey times: data and calculations {#sec-journey-method}

The [journey time analysis](distance.qmd#sec-journeys) routes neighbourhoods to schools on real networks. The code is `R/20_journey_times.R` (the routing, which needs Java 21 and about 40 GB of memory), `R/22_journey_structure.R` (buses, changes, missing a journey and climb), `R/23_school_buses.R` and `R/24_school_bus_penalty.R` (school buses), `R/25_climb.R` (climb across England) and `R/21_journey_analysis.R` (the analysis). They write `data/journey_times.rds`, `data/school_buses.rds` and `data/climb.rds`. Children, deprivation, IDACI and the definition of a school are as [above](#sec-distance-measures).

```{r}
#| include: false
Jm <- readRDS(here::here("data", "journey_times.rds")); SBm <- readRDS(here::here("data", "school_buses.rds")); CBm <- readRDS(here::here("data", "climb.rds"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-journey-sources
#| tbl-cap: "Additional sources for the journey time analysis. All are published and free to download."
tibble::tribble(
  ~Source, ~Publisher, ~`Vintage and unit`, ~`Used for`,
  "<a href='https://download.geofabrik.de/europe/united-kingdom/england.html'>OpenStreetMap county extracts</a>", "OpenStreetMap contributors, via Geofabrik", "Downloaded 8 November 2026", "The street and path network for walking, and for reaching bus stops",
  "<a href='https://data.bus-data.dft.gov.uk/downloads/'>Bus Open Data Service GTFS files</a>", "Department for Transport", "Regional files, downloaded 8 November 2026", "Bus routes and timetables; school buses, from all nine English regions",
  "<a href='https://www.ordnancesurvey.co.uk/products/os-terrain-50'>OS Terrain 50</a>", "Ordnance Survey", "Release of July 2026; a 50 m bare-earth grid", "Slopes, for climb along routes and across England",
  "<a href='https://ipeagit.github.io/r5r/'>r5r 2.3.0</a> and R5", "Pereira and others; Conveyal", "Software", "The routing"
) |> kt(align = "llll", escape = FALSE)
```

**Networks.** Each network holds one OpenStreetMap file, merged with osmosis where an area crosses county extracts, and the bus timetables that serve it, cut to trips that pass within 30 km of the place.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-journey-networks
#| tbl-cap: "The networks. Trips are those running on the routing date, from the timetable files for that network."
Jm$meta |> transmute(Places = places, `OpenStreetMap extracts` = pbfs, `Bus files` = gsub("_", " ", gtfs), `Output Areas` = format(origins, big.mark = ","), Schools = schools, `Bus trips` = format(trips, big.mark = ",")) |> kt(align = "lllrrr")
```

**Choosing bus files.** The regional files follow operators, not places. Portsmouth and Southampton's buses are largely in the South West file, not the South East one. So stops within 3 km of each place's centre were counted in all four files, and each network was given every file with substantial coverage.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-journey-audit
#| tbl-cap: "Bus stops within 3 km of each place's centre, in each regional timetable file."
Jm$audit |> tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = feed, values_from = stops) |> dplyr::rename(Place = place, London = london, `North West` = north_west, `South East` = south_east, `South West` = south_west) |> kt(align = "lrrrr")
```

**Routing date.** `r format(Jm$meta$date[1], "%A %e %B %Y")`, in term time, chosen in advance for every network. Each network's number of trips on that date was checked against nearby Tuesdays to Thursdays, and is close to the highest of them. Early December is low in the current files (127 trips in the Hastings network on 1 December, against 3,398), which is why trips are checked.

**Origins and destinations.** Origins are the `r format(Jm$missing$total, big.mark = ",")` Output Areas in the nine places, at their population-weighted centroids. Destinations are the state secondary schools defined [above](#sec-distance-places), within 15 km of the place's bounding box, so that schools over the boundary count. They include faith and selective schools, as the headline straight-line measure does. `r Jm$missing$total - Jm$missing$routed` Output Area has no route.

**Settings.**

```{r}
#| label: tbl-journey-settings
#| tbl-cap: "The routing scenarios. All use a 120 minute limit on the journey. With buses, walking to and from stops is limited to 60 minutes."
tibble::tribble(
  ~Scenario, ~Modes, ~Departure, ~`Walking speed`, ~Purpose,
  "Walking and bus (headline)", "Walk, bus", "07:45 to 08:15, median", "3.6 km/h", "The usual journey, less dependent on just missing one bus",
  "Walking alone", "Walk", "07:45", "3.6 km/h", "The journey with no bus, and the street network itself",
  "Walking and bus, faster walking", "Walk, bus", "07:45 to 08:15, median", "4.8 km/h", "A check on walking speed",
  "City model's settings", "Walk, bus", "08:00, one departure", "3.6 km/h", "To compare with the city's school system model"
) |> kt(align = "lllll")
```

**From times to measures.** For each Output Area $o$ and scenario, $t_o$ is the time to its quickest school in the set, which need not be the nearest in a straight line. A place's figure for its most deprived third $T$ is

$$M_T = \frac{\sum_{o \in T} w_o t_o}{\sum_{o \in T} w_o}$$

where $w_o$ is the Output Area's 10 to 14 year olds and $T$ is the Output Areas in the third of the place's LSOAs most deprived on Census household deprivation, [as for distance](#sec-distance-measures). The same is done for the rest, and the gap is the difference. The shares over 30 and 45 minutes are child-weighted. IDACI tenths use each Output Area's LSOA, [as above](#sec-distance-measures).

**Journey structure (`R/22_journey_structure.R`).** Each Output Area's journey to its quickest school is rebuilt with `detailed_itineraries`, leaving at 07:45, 08:00 and 08:15, and averaged over the three. Buses per journey counts boardings; a change is a stop between two boardings, and changes are mapped by children to the nearest stop name in the timetable files. The quickest school comes from the walking and bus scenario, so journeys to other schools, and school buses that leave before 07:45, are not counted here.

**Late if missed.** For each Output Area, `expanded_travel_time_matrix` gives the journey for every departure minute from 07:00 to 08:50. With a bell $B$ of 08:45 (08:30 as a check), $L$ is the latest departure that arrives by $B$, and

$$\text{late} = \min_{d > L} (d + \text{time}_d) - B$$

the arrival by the best journey leaving after $L$, whatever that is, including walking. It is small for walkers and frequent routes, and large where a child depends on one infrequent bus.

**School buses (`R/23_school_buses.R`).** From the unfiltered Bus Open Data Service files for all nine English regions, on the routing date. A route counts if it has at most `r SBm$rules$max_trips` trips that day, all starting between 06:30 and 09:30 or between 14:00 and 17:30, with a morning trip that ends, or an afternoon trip that starts, within `r SBm$rules$near_m` metres of a state secondary school and no nearer a [sixth form or further education college](https://get-information-schools.service.gov.uk/Downloads). The school is the nearest one. A route that ends by two schools is credited to one, and timetables do not say who a bus is for. In Brighton and Hove the method finds the routes visible by eye, with `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(SBm$routes$named))` of routes nationally naming a school or similar in their headsign or last stop. Nothing in the files marks term-time only services, so the routing date needs to be in term.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sb-regions
#| tbl-cap: "School buses found, by Bus Open Data Service regional file, on the routing date. Candidates meet the rule on trips and hours. College routes end nearer a college than a school and are left out."
as.data.frame(SBm$regions) |> transmute(Region = gsub("_", " ", region), `Trips that day` = format(trips, big.mark = ","), Routes = format(routes, big.mark = ","), Candidates = candidates, `College routes` = college_routes, `School routes` = school_routes, Schools = schools) |> kt(align = "lrrrrrr")
```

**Missing a school bus (`R/24_school_bus_penalty.R`).** Output Areas within 400 m of a stop on a route's morning trips (before its last stop) are linked to the route's school and routed from 07:00 at each minute with all buses and walking available, so the penalty is by the best real alternative. Bells are not in the data, so $B$ is 15 minutes after the school's last school bus arrives, with a check at 25 minutes. Each school's published start time could replace this: [Longhill's 2023 consultation](https://longhill.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/Timings-of-school-day.pdf) gives 08:20, against 08:19 inferred. Newham and Tower Hamlets have no school routes stopping in them.

**Climb.** r5r's `elevation = "TOBLER"` loaded OS Terrain 50 and reported applying costs, but averaged them across directions and left walking times unchanged in our tests (r5r 2.3.0, R5 7.4), so it is not used. Instead, each walking route is sampled every 50 m and heights are read from Terrain 50. Metres up is the sum of rises along the route, in each direction. Walking time uses Tobler's function, scaled to the routing speed on the flat:

$$v(s) = 3.6 \, \frac{e^{-3.5 |s + 0.05|}}{e^{-3.5 \times 0.05}} \text{ km/h}$$

for slope $s$ in the direction of travel, and is applied to each stretch. Routes are not re-chosen to avoid hills. Terrain 50's 50 m grid smooths short steep streets.

**Climb across England (`R/25_climb.R`).** Heights every 50 m along the straight line from each Output Area in England to its nearest school, from all `r format(CBm$n_tiles, big.mark = ",")` Terrain 50 tiles. In the routed places this correlates at `r sprintf("%.2f", CBm$check$r_out)` (to school) and `r sprintf("%.2f", CBm$check$r_back)` (home) with climb along the route, though it is lower (`r sprintf("%.0f", CBm$check$mean_line_back)` metres against `r sprintf("%.0f", CBm$check$mean_route_back)`, home). The models are as [above](#sec-distance-models): schools within authority with intake and ethnic make-up; IDACI tenths within authority with Census character; and authorities for all three groups given each group's ethnic mix, using the most deprived third's climb.

**Absence.** Authority figures are from DfE's absence by characteristic file. Within-authority models use DfE's absence by pupil residence and IDACI tenth, with effects for each authority and tenth by year, weighted by pupils with errors clustered by authority, as [above](#sec-distance-models) but without Census character, given how few authorities there are.

**Checks and problems found.**

- *Stale networks.* R5 reuses `network.dat` even if its inputs have changed, so the script deletes one older than its inputs.
- *Swapped results.* With walking only and more origins than destinations, r5r searches backwards from destinations and returns the identifiers swapped. That would make a walk go from school to home, which matters with hills. The script routes in batches no larger than the number of schools, and stops if identifiers come back the wrong way round.
- *One file per network.* R5 reads one OpenStreetMap file per folder, so areas crossing county extracts are merged. Brighton and Hove is in the West Sussex extract.
- *Agreement with the city's model.* See [the page](distance.qmd#sec-journey-limits).

## Journeys in the 109 mostly urban authorities: data and calculations {#sec-la-routing-method}

The [109-authority analysis](distance.qmd#sec-la-journeys) repeats the routing above at scale. The code is `R/26_la_networks.R` (networks and their inputs), `R/27_la_routing.R` (routing, one network at a time), `R/28_la_pois.R` (points of interest, [below](#sec-poi-method)) and `R/29_la_analysis.R` (measures and models), with `pipeline/la_resume.sh` and `pipeline/la_pause.sh` to run the routing in stages. Only `R/29`'s output, `data/journey_la.rds`, is committed; the networks and routes run to many gigabytes.

```{r}
#| include: false
library(data.table)
JLm <- readRDS(here::here("data", "journey_la.rds"))
PLm <- JLm$places[JLm$places$in_models == TRUE, ]
```

**Which authorities.** The sample is [R/19's "mostly urban" authorities](#sec-distance-models): at least 80% of children aged 10 to 14 living in urban LSOAs on the ONS 2021 rural-urban classification, and at least 30 LSOAs. That gives `r nrow(PLm)`: `r sum(PLm$london)` London boroughs and `r sum(!PLm$london)` others. Hastings was routed as well, so that the [nine places](distance.qmd#sec-journeys) can be reproduced, but it is a district and has no DfE absence by characteristic, so it is not in the models. In all, `r format(JLm$n_oas, big.mark = ",")` Output Areas were routed.

**Networks.** Neighbouring authorities share a network, so that a child can be routed across a boundary to the nearest school: `r nrow(JLm$nets)` networks, from London's `r format(JLm$nets$oas[JLm$nets$net == "london"], big.mark = ",")` Output Areas in `r JLm$nets$las[JLm$nets$net == "london"]` boroughs to single authorities. Each takes the [OpenStreetMap England extract](https://download.geofabrik.de/europe/united-kingdom/england.html) (Geofabrik, `england-latest.osm.pbf`, 1.71 GB, dated 8 November 2026), clipped with osmosis to a box 30 km beyond its Output Areas, keeping ways that cross the edge. Milton Keynes uses 31 km: at 30 km the edge cut a car park to a single point, and R5 stopped while building park-and-ride areas.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-la-networks
#| tbl-cap: "The 28 networks. Schools are state secondary schools within reach of the network's Output Areas. Bus files are the Bus Open Data Service regional files used."
nm <- JLm$flat_meta[, .(net, schools, feeds = gsub("gtfs_|\\.zip", "", feeds))]
mem <- vapply(names(JLm$members), function(n) if (n == "london") "The 32 London boroughs" else paste(JLm$members[[n]], collapse = ", "), "")
merge(JLm$nets[, .(net, las, oas)], nm, by = "net")[order(-oas)][, .(Network = gsub("_", " ", net), Authorities = mem[net], `Output Areas` = format(oas, big.mark = ","), Schools = schools, `Bus files` = gsub("_", " ", feeds))] |> kt(align = "llrrl")
```

**Bus files.** The Department for Transport's [Bus Open Data Service](https://data.bus-data.dft.gov.uk/downloads/) publishes GTFS timetables by region, but the regions follow operators, not places. So stops in every regional file were counted within 5 km of each network's box, and a network takes every file with at least 50 such stops and at least 2% of the largest count. Each file is clipped to the network's box plus 30 km with `gtfstools`. One file needed repair: in the South East file, Sullivan Buses route 84 is written as two frequency-based trips (every 20 minutes from 09:25 to 13:05), which `r5r`'s detailed itineraries cannot use. They were converted to timetabled trips with `gtfstools::frequencies_to_stop_times`, adding 22 trips to six networks. Journey times rerun after the change were identical to those before it.

**Routing.** As [for the nine places](#sec-journey-method), with r5r 2.3.0 and Java 21, on Tuesday `r format(JLm$flat_meta$date[1], "%e %B %Y")`, in term. Each network runs in its own process, saving after each step:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-la-steps
#| tbl-cap: "The routing steps for each network. Walking speed is 3.6 km/h except where stated. Trips are limited to 120 minutes and walking within a bus journey to 60."
tibble::tribble(
  ~Step, ~What, ~Measures,
  "Journey times", "Walking and bus, departures 07:45 to 08:15 (the median); walking alone; walking and bus at 4.8 km/h (not London, for memory)", "Minutes to the quickest school, the three quickest and the quickest neither selective nor faith; schools within 30 and 45 minutes",
  "Journey structure", "The journey to the quickest school by walking and bus, leaving at 07:45, 08:00 and 08:15", "Walking only, one bus, two or more; buses per journey; minutes waiting; stops where children board, change and alight",
  "Walking route", "The route on foot to the quickest school on foot, as a line", "Metres climbed each way, from OS Terrain 50 every 50 m; walking time by Tobler's function",
  "Missing a journey", "Every departure minute from 07:00, with a bell at 08:45 (08:30 as a check)", "The last departure that arrives by the bell, and minutes late on the best journey after it"
) |> kt(align = "lll")
```

London ran alone, with a 52 GB Java heap and six threads; other networks used 18 GB and five. `r format(sum(JLm$no_route$no_bus), big.mark = ",")` Output Areas have no route by walking and bus and `r format(sum(JLm$no_route$no_walk), big.mark = ",")` none on foot within the limits, mostly on the rural edges of large authorities; they are left out of the averages.

**From routes to measures.** For each authority, each measure $m_o$ for Output Area $o$ is averaged over the most deprived third of its neighbourhoods $T$ and over the rest, weighted by children aged 10 to 14, [as for the nine places](#sec-journey-method):

$$M_T = \frac{\sum_{o \in T} w_o m_o}{\sum_{o \in T} w_o}$$

The gap is $M_T - M_{\text{rest}}$. Two other splits check the result. For children in income-deprived families, each Output Area's children are split by its LSOA's IDACI rate $r_o$, so the weights are $w_o r_o$ and $w_o (1 - r_o)$. For England's most deprived three tenths, $T$ is the LSOAs in IDACI tenths 1 to 3 nationally. Minutes per kilometre is the deprived third's mean minutes divided by its mean straight-line distance.

**Is Brighton and Hove unusual?** Each measure is ranked across the `r nrow(PLm)` authorities, and across the `r sum(!PLm$london)` outside London. To ask whether the city is unusual *given* its distance, each measure is regressed across authorities on the matching straight-line distance (and density, for changes of bus), and the city's studentised residual is compared with the others'.

**Reproduction.** The nine places' journey times were recomputed in the new networks. For Brighton and Hove, Blackpool, Bristol, Hastings, Newham, Plymouth, Portsmouth, Southampton and Tower Hamlets, the deprived third, the rest and the gap are identical to [those above](distance.qmd#tbl-journeys).

**The models.** Three designs, each with its own weaknesses, as for straight-line distance:

- *Authorities.* DfE's [absence by pupil characteristics](https://explore-education-statistics.service.gov.uk/data-catalogue/data-set/e2eb493a-dc95-41f4-96ef-b886c5cd2019), secondary and primary, for disadvantaged, non-disadvantaged and all pupils, 2018/19 and 2020/21 to 2024/25. Each group's absence is regressed on the deprived third's journey measure with year effects and errors clustered by authority. Controls are added in four sets: the share of pupils disadvantaged and how urban the authority is; then the group's ethnic mix (shares White British, Asian, Black and mixed heritage, from DfE's [free school meals by ethnicity](https://explore-education-statistics.service.gov.uk/find-statistics/school-pupils-and-their-characteristics)); then region; then seven Census measures (graduates, bad health, White British residents, social renting, no car, deprivation and density) and six of pupils (special needs support, education, health and care plans, prior attainment, English as an additional language, White British and mobility). "Given km" adds straight-line distance from the deprived third.
- *Tenths within authorities.* DfE's [absence by pupil residence and IDACI tenth](https://explore-education-statistics.service.gov.uk/data-catalogue/data-set/6dd7f70e-440f-4c0f-b8d1-056678c25301), all pupils, 2023/24 and 2024/25. Each tenth of each authority takes the child-weighted mean journey of its Output Areas. Effects for each authority in each year and each tenth in each year, weighted by pupils, with errors clustered by authority. Census character is as [above](#sec-distance-models).
- *Schools within authorities.* Each school's "nearest children" are those whose quickest school it is, and a school needs at least 100 of them. Autumn and spring 2025/26 absence for all pupils, with authority effects and the intake controls of the [straight-line school models](#sec-distance-models): free school meals, English as an additional language, White British share, prior attainment, neighbourhood education, special needs, mobility, single-sex, age range and kind of place. Distance enters as the doubling of the mean straight-line distance of those children. Selective schools are left out.

Measures are reported for one standard deviation more, so that minutes, shares and metres can be compared, and the samples are repeated without London and without Brighton and Hove.

**What this cannot do.** The timetables are buses only. They miss the Underground, Overground, Elizabeth line and DLR in London, Metrolink, the Tyne and Wear Metro, West Midlands Metro, Supertram, Nottingham's trams and local rail, all of which would shorten journeys where they run. Journeys go to the quickest school, not the one attended, and bells are assumed. Deprivation is of the neighbourhood, and absence by disadvantage is published only for whole authorities.

## Points of interest on the way: data and calculations {#sec-poi-method}

`R/28_la_pois.R` takes points of interest from the same OpenStreetMap extract as the networks (dated `r format(JLm$poi$osm_date, "%e %B %Y")`), with `osmextract`, and counts them along each journey of `R/27`.

**What counts.** Five groups, from OpenStreetMap's own tags. Schools, transport, parking and street furniture are left out. Things mapped as areas are represented by a point inside them, except open spaces, which keep their outlines, because a child walks past the edge of a park, not its middle.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-poi-tags
#| tbl-cap: !expr paste0(format(JLm$poi$n, big.mark = ","), " points of interest in England. The commonest tags in each group are shown, with counts.")
TG <- c(food_drink = "Food and drink", shops = "Shops", leisure = "Leisure", open_space = "Open space", civic = "Civic")
DEF <- c(food_drink = "amenity = cafe, fast_food, restaurant, pub, bar, ice_cream, food_court, biergarten",
         shops = "any shop, except vacant or disused",
         leisure = "cinemas, theatres, arts centres, nightclubs, gambling, arcades, bowling, sports and fitness centres, swimming pools, ice rinks, trampoline and water parks, museums, galleries, attractions, viewpoints, zoos",
         open_space = "leisure = park, playground, recreation_ground, common, nature_reserve, dog_park; beaches",
         civic = "libraries, community and youth centres, places of worship, town halls, post offices, banks, pharmacies, doctors, dentists, clinics, hospitals, police and fire stations, courts, markets")
bc <- JLm$poi$by_cat[, .(n = sum(n)), by = cat]
tt <- JLm$poi$top_tags[, .(top = paste(sprintf("%s (%s)", gsub("_", " ", tag), format(n, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)), collapse = ", ")), by = cat]
merge(bc, tt, by = "cat")[match(names(TG), cat)][, .(Group = TG[cat], Tags = DEF[cat], `In England` = format(n, big.mark = ","), Commonest = top)] |> kt(align = "llrl")
```

**Where they are counted.** For every Output Area's journey to its quickest school, and each departure at 07:45, 08:00 and 08:15:

- *Around stops:* points of interest within 200 metres of the stop where the journey starts, of each stop where it changes bus, and of the stop where it ends. A journey that changes twice adds the counts at both changes. 400 metres is a check.
- *Along walking:* within 50 metres of the whole walking route to the quickest school on foot, and of the walking legs of the 08:00 bus journey. 100 metres is a check.
- *Around home:* within 400 metres of the Output Area's centroid, as a control.

Counts are averaged over the three departures. A journey with no change has none at changes, so the change measure mixes how often children change with how busy the changes are; a model with the share needing two or more buses and the number of buses held constant separates them.

**Measures and models.** Each authority's deprived third, each IDACI tenth within an authority and each school's nearest children take the child-weighted mean count, as for journey times, and enter the same three designs [above](#sec-la-routing-method), with points of interest near home added as a control in the within-authority design.

**Limits.** OpenStreetMap's coverage of shops and cafés varies from place to place and is usually fuller in cities, so a count partly measures how well a place is mapped. A point of interest is not a reason to stay off school, and nothing here says what children did there.

## From absence to GCSE results: data and calculations {#sec-gcse-method}

`R/30_distance_gcse.R` writes `data/distance_gcse.rds` for [the GCSE section](distance.qmd#sec-gcse).

```{r}
#| include: false
GCm <- readRDS(here::here("data", "distance_gcse.rds"))
```

**Results.** Attainment 8 for disadvantaged, non-disadvantaged and all pupils, by school, from the [KS4 performance tables](https://www.compare-school-performance.service.gov.uk/download-data) for 2021/22 to 2024/25, as in [the model](#sec-full-spec). An authority's figure for each group is the mean of its schools' figures weighted by the number of pupils in that group at the end of KS4, and the same for Progress 8.

**The chain.** The [authority model](#sec-la-routing-method) gives $\beta_{km}$, points of absence per kilometre for each group, here fitted on the years with results. Value Added v2.1 models log Attainment 8 on log absence with elasticity $\varepsilon$ (`r sprintf("%.3f", GCm$means$elasticity[GCm$means$g == "dis"])` for disadvantaged pupils, `r sprintf("%.3f", GCm$means$elasticity[GCm$means$g == "non"])` non-disadvantaged, `r sprintf("%.3f", GCm$means$elasticity[GCm$means$g == "all"])` all). At a group's mean Attainment 8 $\bar{A}$ and absence $\bar{a}$ across the `r GCm$n_las` authorities, a point of absence is worth $\bar{A} \varepsilon / \bar{a}$ points, and the chain is

$$\Delta A_{km} = \beta_{km} \times \frac{\bar{A} \, \varepsilon}{\bar{a}}$$

The v2.1 elasticity is for a school's absence of all pupils, so applying it to a group's own absence assumes that a point of absence costs the group's pupils what it costs a school. As a check, the second link is also estimated across the authorities, by the slope of each group's Attainment 8 on its own absence with the same controls. That gives a smaller chain. The interval for the chain reflects the first link only, because the second is estimated far more precisely.

**The direct check.** Each group's Attainment 8, and Progress 8, regressed on the same distance with the same controls, years and clustering. Between schools, each school's Attainment 8 for each group on the doubling of its nearest children's distance, within authority, with the intake controls of [the school design](#sec-la-routing-method).

**The mixing estimate on the same scale.** Gorard and Siddiqui (2019) model capped KS4 points (each pupil's best eight GCSEs or equivalents) for the `r format(GCm$gorard$n, big.mark = ",")` pupils who finished KS4 in `r GCm$gorard$cohort`: mean `r GCm$gorard$mean_capped`, standard deviation `r GCm$gorard$sd_capped` between pupils (their Table 1). On that scale a grade is 6 points (C = 40, B = 46), so a grade higher in all eight subjects is 48 points. Attainment 8 counts English and maths twice, ten weights in all, and a grade is one point in each, so a grade higher in all subjects is 10 points. One Attainment 8 point is therefore about `r GCm$gorard$capped_per_att8` capped points, and their standard deviation is about `r sprintf("%.1f", GCm$gorard$sd_att8)` Attainment 8 points. Their 0.05 to 0.15 is then `r sprintf("%.1f", GCm$gorard$att8[["lo"]])` to `r sprintf("%.1f", GCm$gorard$att8[["hi"]])` points. DfE's [2016 key figures](https://dera.ioe.ac.uk/27618/1/Progress_8_key_figures_2016_V1.0.pdf) give the standard deviation of pupils' Progress 8 scores as `r GCm$gorard$p8_sd_2016` a slot, or `r sprintf("%.1f", 10 * GCm$gorard$p8_sd_2016)` Attainment 8 points: the spread left once prior attainment is known. On that narrower scale the range is `r sprintf("%.1f", GCm$gorard$att8_p8scale[["lo"]])` to `r sprintf("%.1f", GCm$gorard$att8_p8scale[["hi"]])`. Their outcome is the raw score, so the first conversion is the right one; the second shows how much it depends on the scale. The 2015 GCSEs were graded A* to G, and today's 9 to 1 scale is not the same, so this is approximate.

Gorard and Siddiqui do not show how the range is derived. It matches the size of their standardised school composition coefficients at the end of KS4, such as `r GCm$gorard$coefs_y11[["School mean points score"]]` for the school's mean points score and `r GCm$gorard$coefs_y11[["Always-FSM segregation for school"]]` for its segregation of always-disadvantaged pupils, which are per standard deviation of the school measure.

**Limits.** The chain multiplies two associations, both between places or schools, so it is what distance would cost if both were causal. Authority figures for a group average over very different schools, and the direct check has wide intervals.

## What the admissions changes did: data and calculations {#sec-admissions-method}

`R/31_admissions_journeys.R` writes `data/admissions_journeys.rds` for [the admissions section](distance.qmd#sec-admissions).

```{r}
#| include: false
AJm <- readRDS(here::here("data", "admissions_journeys.rds"))
```

**Source.** The published scenario runs of [the city's school system model](https://adamdennett.github.io/bh-school-system/), `data/council_options.rds` in [its repository](https://github.com/`r AJm$source$repo`), downloaded at commit `r substr(AJm$source$commit, 1, 7)` (model run of `r format(AJm$source$model_built, "%e %B %Y")`). The model allocates each year's applicants to the city's schools under a given catchment map and set of priorities, with journeys routed by r5r over OpenStreetMap and bus timetables. Its disadvantaged children are placed using `r AJm$source$dis_source`. How it is built and checked is set out in its own documentation; nothing is refitted here.

**The runs.** *Today* is the 2024 catchment map with today's priorities, including priority 6 at 5%. *The pre-2024 catchments* keeps today's priorities on the earlier map. *Today, without priority 6* keeps the map and drops the priority. The map's effect $\Delta_{\text{map}}$ is today minus the pre-2024 run, and priority 6's $\Delta_{6}$ is today minus the run without it. The model has no run with both undone, so their joint effect is taken as $\Delta_{\text{map}} + \Delta_{6}$. The 2026 entry year is used; 2030 is similar.

**Measures.** Journeys are the model's mean walking and bus minutes from home to the school offered, weighted by children, for the city's schools, for disadvantaged children ($t_D$), for others, and for all. Mixing is the model's Gorard index of disadvantaged children across the city's modelled intakes, $G$.

**On the Attainment 8 scale.** A change in journeys $\Delta t$ is costed two ways. Through distance, $\Delta t$ is divided by the `r sprintf("%.1f", AJm$mpk)` minutes per straight-line kilometre of Brighton and Hove's deprived journeys ([above](#sec-la-routing-method)) and multiplied by the chain per kilometre for disadvantaged pupils ([above](#sec-gcse-method)), from all 109 authorities and from those outside London. Through time, $\Delta t$ is multiplied by the authority model's points of absence per minute for disadvantaged pupils with every control (`r sprintf("%.3f", AJm$per_min[["All 109"]])` for all 109, `r sprintf("%.3f", AJm$per_min[["Without London"]])` outside London) and by `r sprintf("%.2f", AJm$per_point)` Attainment 8 points per point of absence. The range in the text spans the four. The mixing gain assumes that Gorard and Siddiqui's 0.05 to 0.15 of a standard deviation, for intakes as mixed as possible ($G = 0$), applies in proportion to the segregation removed:

$$\text{gain} = \frac{-\Delta G}{G_{\text{before}}} \times (1.0 \text{ to } 3.1)$$

Attainment 8 points. Nothing in their paper says the gain is proportional, so this is an assumption made to put the two on one scale.

**Limits.** The model's journeys are to the school offered on national offer day, not the school attended in September, and its disadvantaged children are modelled, not observed. Averages hide the children whose journeys changed most. The change in the index is close to the size the model's own documentation treats as within its uncertainty.

## The proposals that did not go ahead: data and calculations {#sec-proposals-method}

`R/32_admissions_proposals.R` writes `data/admissions_proposals.rds` for [the proposals section](distance.qmd#sec-proposals).

```{r}
#| include: false
APm <- readRDS(here::here("data", "admissions_proposals.rds"))
```

**The model.** The school system model has no published runs of these proposals, so they are run on the model itself rather than on its outputs. Its simulator code and inputs, `r and_list(paste0("<code>", APm$source$files, "</code>"))`, are downloaded from [its repository](https://github.com/`r APm$source$repo`) at commit `r substr(APm$source$commit, 1, 7)`, the version whose published runs [R/31 uses](#sec-admissions-method), and run unchanged under today's map and priorities. As a check, the script first runs today's arrangements and compares them with the model's own published run of today: the segregation index and both journey measures are `r if (max(abs(APm$check$gorard - APm$check$g_pub), abs(APm$check$dep_min - APm$check$d_pub), abs(APm$check$mean_min - APm$check$m_pub)) < 1e-9) "identical" else "within a millionth"` in 2026 and 2030, and the script stops if they differ by more than a millionth.

**The runs.** Each changes only what the proposal changes: the priority 6 share (5% today; 20% in the council's proposal; 30%, with the same cuts, as Class Divide proposed), and the admission numbers of Dorothy Stringer and Blatchington Mill, each cut by 30 from `r APm$pan_now[[1]]` to `r APm$pan_now[[1]] - 30`. The parts of the council's proposal are also run separately, and the priority 6 share is swept from 0 to 40%, with and without the cuts, to find where it stops binding. The measures are those of [the published runs](#sec-admissions-method), plus the children displaced from their catchment school and the places taken under priority 6, as the model defines them. Effects are against today in the same year, and are put on the Attainment 8 scale [as above](#sec-admissions-method).

**Limits.** The model's demand for places holds families' preferences as they are. A larger share might draw more applications from the single-school catchments than the model allows, so the ceiling it finds is for today's preferences. Everything else in [the limits above](#sec-admissions-method) applies.

## Whose journeys changed: data and calculations {#sec-neighbourhoods-method}

`R/33_admissions_neighbourhoods.R` writes `data/admissions_neighbourhoods.rds` for [the neighbourhood section](distance.qmd#sec-admissions-neighbourhoods). It runs the same model, at the same commit, as [R/32](#sec-proposals-method), for the pre-2024 catchments, today, and the council's 2024 proposal, all for 2026 entry under today's priorities.

**Zones.** The model's origins are zones: Census LSOAs, or where a catchment boundary crosses an LSOA, the parts on either side. Each zone's catchment on each map comes from the model's own designs, so a zone is grouped by how the 2024 map moved it: out of Longhill's catchment into Stringer and Varndean's, the other way, other changes, or unchanged. Zones are named by the [House of Commons Library's MSOA names](https://houseofcommonslibrary.github.io/msoanames/) (version 2.2), through the ONS 2021 LSOA to MSOA lookup.

**Measures.** For each zone and run: the children the model places (a year's applicants), its modelled disadvantaged children (as for [the city figures](#sec-admissions-method)), the mean walking and bus minutes to the school offered at the city's schools for all of them and for the disadvantaged children, and the shares offered Longhill and Dorothy Stringer or Varndean. Groups take means weighted by children, or by disadvantaged children for their journeys. Whitehawk's cost in Attainment 8 points is costed [as above](#sec-admissions-method), from its disadvantaged children's change in minutes.

**Limits.** Zones hold a few children a year each, as the model places them, so single zones are not reported on their own. The model's children are spread over schools in proportion to its probabilities, so a zone's journey is an average over where its children might go. Applying a link measured across authorities to one neighbourhood is an extrapolation.

# Data

Every school's v2.0 value added, for every group, with intervals and the
within-authority version, is in
[va_v2_schools.csv](data/va_v2_schools.csv). Inputs are the DfE
performance tables, school census and absence data, GIAS, the 2021 Census
and Ofsted's monthly management information, downloaded and assembled by
this repository's own pipeline (`R/00_fetch_data.R`, from the
[original project](https://github.com/adamdennett/school_attainment_tool)'s
scripts). Ofsted judgements are refreshed each month. The build is described in the
[repository README](https://github.com/adamdennett/school_value_added#readme).
